Women, sexual minority respondents, and White respondents reported higher odds across all four outcomes than their peers, and the researchers found further differences at the intersections of race, sex and sexual orientation. One important limitation: these are separate cross-sectional snapshots, not the same people followed over time, so the study can show that the young adult population looks more anxious than it did in 2020, but not why, and rising diagnosis and medication numbers can partly reflect better recognition and access rather than more illness.

title: Do anti-stigma trainings for doctors and nurses actually work?
blurb: Pooling 21 randomized controlled trials, educational anti-stigma programs modestly reduced healthcare workers' negative attitudes toward people with mental illness right after training (SMD = -0.38). Knowledge and willingness to be near patients did not improve, and the attitude gains were not maintained at follow-up.
summary: Hospitals and universities run a lot of anti-stigma workshops, and this review asked whether they change anything. The authors searched five research databases through July 2025 and pulled together every randomized controlled trial that tested an educational program aimed at reducing mental health stigma among healthcare professionals or students in training. Nineteen reports covering 21 studies made the cut. Immediately after training, participants scored meaningfully lower on explicit negative attitudes toward people with mental illness, with a pooled effect size of -0.38 (a small-to-moderate difference). Practicing clinicians also reported stronger intentions to behave differently, though students did not. But the picture gets thinner from there. Mental health knowledge did not improve. Neither did 'social distance,' the measure of how comfortable someone is living or working near a person with mental illness. And where studies followed up weeks or months later, the early gains had faded. The honest limitation is one the authors flag themselves: using the GRADE system, the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, the trials used inconsistent outcome measures, and most looked only at what people said on a questionnaire, not at how they actually treated patients.

title: Does cannabis actually calm you down?
blurb: In a double-blind trial, 120 regular cannabis users vaped placebo, 20 mg THC, or 40 mg THC. Self-reported stress dropped about equally in all three groups, while heart rate rose significantly more on the high dose than on placebo.
summary: Stress relief is one of the most common reasons people give for using cannabis. This trial put that belief to a controlled test, and it is the first to track several stress systems at once. Researchers randomly assigned 120 regular cannabis users (56 men, 52 women, 12 non-binary or transgender participants) to vape one of three things without knowing which: placebo, a moderate 20 mg dose of THC, or a high 40 mg dose. Neither participants nor the researchers running the session knew the assignment. Stress ratings and saliva cortisol were collected before vaping, five minutes after, and an hour after, while a wristband continuously logged heart rate, heart rate variability, and skin conductance. The subjective result is the striking one: people reported feeling less stressed after vaping, but so did the placebo group, and by about the same amount, which points to expectancy rather than the drug. Physiologically, the picture split apart. Cortisol dropped more sharply on the high dose, and skin conductance responses dampened in both cannabis groups, but heart rate rose more on the high dose than on placebo. A key limitation: participants were all regular users tested in a lab, so this says little about occasional users or real-world stressful moments.

title: Can one day of an inhaled psychedelic lift treatment-resistant depression?
blurb: In a phase 2b trial across 16 European sites, 81 adults with treatment-resistant depression received up to three escalating inhaled doses of mebufotenin (GH001) or placebo on a single day. One week later, 57.5% of the drug group (23 of 40) were in remission, compared with 0% of the 41 placebo patients.
summary: Most people with treatment-resistant depression have already tried several antidepressants without much relief, so researchers keep looking for something that works faster and differently. This trial tested GH001, a synthetic inhaled form of mebufotenin (also known as 5-MeO-DMT, a short-acting psychedelic). Eighty-one adults aged 18 to 64 who had not responded to two to five previous antidepressants were randomly assigned, double-blind, to receive either GH001 or a matching placebo. Everything happened on a single day: participants got an individualized regimen of up to three escalating doses (6, 12, and 18 mg), then were followed for a week. On the standard depression rating scale, the GH001 group improved by about 15.5 points more than placebo, an unusually large effect. By day 8, 23 of 40 GH001 patients met the threshold for remission, while none of the 41 placebo patients did. No severe or serious adverse events were reported during the placebo-controlled period. The honest limitation: this is a small, one-week trial, and a drug that produces a vivid psychedelic experience is very hard to blind, so participants likely guessed which group they were in. The trial was also funded by the company developing the drug, and several authors are employees or shareholders. Longer, larger trials will decide whether the effect holds up.

title: Do antidepressants in pregnancy raise a child's risk of autism or ADHD?
blurb: A meta-analysis pooled 37 studies covering 648,626 antidepressant-exposed pregnancies and 24,967,806 unexposed ones. Raw estimates showed 35% higher ADHD risk and 69% higher autism risk in exposed children, but the associations shrank or disappeared once confounding was accounted for, and fathers' antidepressant use during pregnancy showed a similar pattern.
summary: This is one of the most common worries in perinatal psychiatry: is it safe to stay on an antidepressant while pregnant? Researchers searched four databases through May 2025 and pooled 37 studies comparing children born after prenatal antidepressant exposure with children who were not exposed, covering roughly 650,000 exposed and 25 million unexposed pregnancies. At first glance, the numbers look worrying: exposed children had about 35% higher relative risk of ADHD and 69% higher relative risk of autism. But the team then pushed on those numbers. Higher doses were not linked to higher autism risk. Exposure before conception, when the drug could not have reached the fetus, showed similar associations. And in the study's clever check, fathers' antidepressant use during pregnancy was also tied to more ADHD and autism in the children, which points toward shared family, genetic, and illness-related explanations rather than the medication itself. In analyses that adjusted for maternal mental illness and familial factors, most associations weakened or lost significance, and no specific SSRI or SNRI stood out. The authors rated the certainty of evidence as low to very low, and note that observational data can never fully rule out confounding. Their stated interpretation is that antidepressant treatment should continue for pregnant women with moderate-to-severe depression.

title: Does a parent's depression drag down a kid's grades?
blurb: Researchers tracked about 9,000 families in the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Study and compared cousins to strip out shared family background. Small links between parents' psychiatric symptoms and children's 5th-grade test scores disappeared once cousins were compared.
summary: It is a familiar assumption that a parent's anxiety, depression, ADHD, eating disorder, or drinking problem will show up in their child's report card. This study asked whether that link is actually causal. Using roughly 9,000 families from the large Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Study, researchers had parents report their own symptoms during pregnancy and again during the child's childhood. The children then took Norway's nationally standardized 5th-grade tests in math, reading comprehension, and English at about age 10. The clever part is the design: instead of comparing unrelated families, the team compared children who are cousins, so that everything siblings-turned-parents share (genes, upbringing, neighborhood, social class) is held constant. In the ordinary analysis, more parental symptoms went with slightly lower reading and math scores, but the effects were tiny, with standardized betas between -0.060 and -0.013. In the cousin comparison, those associations were no longer statistically significant. The authors read this as evidence that parental symptoms do not directly move a child's achievement much on their own. One honest limitation: the families who could be included in the cousin analysis differed from the full sample, so the results may not generalize cleanly to all families, and the design cannot rule out very small effects.

title: Pesticides in pregnancy and autism traits: a big study finds no link
blurb: Researchers measured organophosphate pesticide breakdown products in the urine of 3,339 pregnant women across 20 US sites and later scored their children's autism-related traits. After full adjustment, prenatal exposure showed no association with those traits.
summary: Organophosphate pesticides are known neurotoxins, and most Americans get low-level exposure through food, so the worry that prenatal exposure might contribute to autism has circulated for years with inconsistent evidence behind it. This analysis pooled harmonized data from 20 study sites in the US ECHO cohort, following mother-child pairs recruited between 1997 and 2019. Scientists measured two markers of organophosphate exposure in the mothers' urine during pregnancy: TCPy and the sum of six dialkyl phosphate metabolites. Years later, parents rated their children on the Social Responsiveness Scale, a standard measure of autism-related traits, at an average age of 6.4 years. Among the 3,339 pairs, crude models actually hinted at slightly lower autism trait scores with higher exposure, but once the researchers adjusted for maternal demographics, behavior, and diet, the associations shrank to nothing, for example a beta of -0.13 (95% CI -0.57 to 0.31) per doubling of TCPy. Results held across boys and girls and across several alternative statistical approaches, and diet quality did not change the picture. Limitations worth noting: exposure came from spot urine samples, which reflect recent intake rather than a whole pregnancy, autism traits were parent-reported rather than clinically diagnosed, and the exposure range studied was typical dietary levels, not occupational ones.

title: Can a self-paced online program treat PTSD from childhood trauma?
blurb: 181 adults with PTSD linked to childhood interpersonal trauma tried an online program combining self-guided modules with optional virtual group sessions. It beat standard care on symptom reduction, with benefits still holding four months later.
summary: Adults whose PTSD traces back to childhood abuse or other interpersonal trauma often struggle to access specialized treatment, especially outside major cities. This trial tested "Trauma PORTAL," a hybrid program combining eight self-paced online psychoeducation and skills modules with eight optional one-hour virtual group sessions led by trauma therapists. Researchers in Ontario, Canada randomly assigned 181 adults (81% women, average age 41) with PTSD from childhood interpersonal trauma to either Trauma PORTAL or standard care. After eight weeks, the program group's PTSD symptoms (measured on the PCL-5 scale) had dropped about 7 points more than the standard-care group, a moderate effect, and that gap held steady at the 16-week follow-up. No adverse events were reported. The main limitation is that this was a single site with an assessor-blind but not participant-blind design, and it compared the program to routine care rather than to an existing gold-standard trauma therapy, so it shows the approach works better than doing nothing in particular, not that it matches specialized in-person treatment.

title: Bipolar Disorder May Rewire the Brain's Communication Network
blurb: Scans of 449 people with bipolar disorder and 510 controls across 16 sites found less efficient, more roundabout brain wiring in emotion and reward circuits, with the disruption tracking illness duration and severity.
summary: Using diffusion MRI, which maps the brain's white-matter wiring, an international team examined structural connectivity in 449 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder and 510 healthy controls across 16 research sites worldwide, coordinated through the ENIGMA Bipolar Disorder Working Group. Rather than looking at single brain regions, they modeled the brain as a network and measured how efficiently different regions communicate with each other. People with bipolar disorder showed less densely connected networks, longer communication paths between regions, and greater reliance on a small number of 'hub' regions to relay signals -- changes concentrated in circuits tied to emotion regulation, reward processing, and memory, including connections between the amygdala, hippocampus, and frontal cortex. These network disruptions were more pronounced in people with longer illness duration, later age of first episode, and a history of psychosis, while a higher number of past manic episodes was linked to unexpectedly stronger connectivity in some emotion-related circuits. Common medications, including antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and antipsychotics, were associated with reduced connectivity in some circuits, though the effect of lithium was unclear. Because the study captured each person's brain at a single point in time rather than tracking them over years, the researchers can't say whether these network changes cause worsening symptoms, result from them, or simply reflect medication exposure -- only that they travel together.

title: Do more risk genes mean more severe schizophrenia?
blurb: Researchers compared 346 people hospitalized continuously for at least five years with treatment-resistant schizophrenia against more than 18,000 others. Each standard-deviation rise in schizophrenia polygenic score raised the odds of being in that most severe group by 40% to 80%.
summary: More than one in five people with schizophrenia get little or no benefit from antipsychotic medication, and a smaller group stays severely ill for years on end. Researchers asked whether that most severe form carries a heavier load of the common genetic variants linked to schizophrenia. They recruited 346 people of European ancestry from Pennsylvania state psychiatric hospitals who met a strict definition: at least five years of continuous hospitalization, active treatment, and no response to three or more antipsychotics. They compared them with 10,757 people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, 1,148 with schizophrenia generally, and 6,320 people without psychiatric diagnoses, drawn from cohorts in the US, Sweden, and the UK, for 18,571 people in total. For each standard-deviation increase in schizophrenia polygenic score, the odds of being in the continuously hospitalized group rose by 40% to 80% relative to the other schizophrenia groups. A smaller exploratory analysis in 476 people of African ancestry (78 cases) pointed in the same direction with weaker statistical support. The pattern held after accounting for sex and after excluding people with additional diagnoses. Limits worth naming: the comparison groups came from different countries and recruitment settings, which can introduce differences that have nothing to do with genetics; the effect describes group averages rather than any individual's prognosis; and polygenic scores still perform poorly outside European-ancestry samples.

title: A Polish Version of the 'Dark Tetrad' Test Mostly Holds Up, With One Weak Spot
blurb: A 931-person validation of the Polish Short Dark Tetrad found the sadism and psychopathy scales performed well, but the Machiavellianism subscale showed weak internal reliability (alpha = .67).
summary: The Short Dark Tetrad (SD4) is a brief 28-item questionnaire used to measure four socially aversive personality traits: subclinical psychopathy, narcissism, Machiavellianism, and sadism. Because psychological tools built in one language and culture don't always translate cleanly, researchers led by Pawel Debski adapted the SD4 for Polish speakers and tested it on 931 adults (average age about 35, roughly three-quarters women) recruited online. Using split-sample statistical testing, meaning the sample was divided so one half could generate a model and the other half could confirm it, the team compared several ways the four traits might fit together. A model that included both trait-specific scales and one broader underlying "dark personality" factor fit the data best. Most subscales showed acceptable reliability, and the sadism items in particular lined up well with an established sadism measure, supporting the tool's validity. However, the Machiavellianism subscale showed weaker internal consistency (alpha = .67), meaning its items didn't hang together as tightly as the other traits' items did. The authors conclude the Polish SD4 is usable as a brief dark-personality screener but say results from the Machiavellianism scale, and comparisons between men and women, should be interpreted cautiously. The sample was an online convenience sample with a gender imbalance and no formal back-translation check, which limits how confidently the findings generalize.

title: Two PTSD therapies work. Which works better depends on which studies you keep.
blurb: A meta-analysis of 163 studies and 48,841 people found both Prolonged Exposure and Cognitive Processing Therapy produced large PTSD symptom reductions (Hedges' g = 1.67), but no patient characteristic predicted which therapy worked better until ten unusual studies were removed.
summary: Prolonged Exposure (PE) and Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) are the two most widely implemented talking treatments for PTSD, and guidelines recommend both. What clinicians still cannot answer is which to offer a particular person. Researchers led by Bingyu Xu screened 5,188 records and pooled 175 treatment arms from 163 studies covering 48,841 participants, then used meta-regression, a method that tests whether study characteristics predict how large an effect a study found, to ask whether the answer depends on age, sex, trauma type, or whether the sample was military or civilian. Pooled across everything, symptom reduction was large: Hedges' g = 1.67, meaning a shift of about one and two-thirds standard deviations. But in the full sample not one moderator mattered, and neither did any interaction with treatment type: statistically, there was no evidence either therapy suited any group better. That changed only after the team removed ten effect sizes flagged as statistical outliers, mostly small studies reporting implausibly large effects, one of them g = 13.48. In that trimmed analysis the overall effect settled at g = 1.55 and PE was associated with larger effects than CPT in non-military samples. Dropout was similar either way, averaging 22.9% for PE and 25.6% for CPT. So the headline about civilians rests on a judgement call about which studies to exclude, and the authors say as much, calling treatment-comparison findings "sensitive to influential outlying effects." Two further cautions: heterogeneity was extreme (I-squared = 98%), so the studies disagreed far more than chance explains, and only 27 of the 163 were randomised trials with an inactive control while 75 had no control group at all, meaning much of that large effect reflects people improving during treatment rather than because of it.

title: How common is treatment-resistant schizophrenia? Japan's largest study says 28.6%
blurb: Across 205 Japanese hospitals and 18,914 discharged patients, 28.6% of those formally assessed for treatment resistance met criteria -- but only 52.2% were ever assessed, and fewer than half of those identified were prescribed clozapine.
summary: When schizophrenia does not respond to two adequate trials of antipsychotic medication it is classified as treatment-resistant, and that label matters because it is the gateway to clozapine, the one drug with established benefit for these patients. How many people fall into this group is the number behind staffing, training and drug policy, and it has never been well established. Researchers led by Yusuke Arai used Japan's EGUIDE project data, covering patients with schizophrenia discharged from 205 institutions between 2016 and 2024, and applied Japan's standardised criteria. Of 18,914 patients, 9,870 underwent a formal treatment-resistance assessment, and of those, 2,819 met criteria: a prevalence of 28.6%. That sits well below the 36.7% pooled estimate from an earlier meta-analysis of 50 studies, but almost exactly on the 28.4% that same review found among its lowest-risk-of-bias studies, which the authors argue is the fair comparison. A second number matters more: of the 2,819 identified, only 46.4% were prescribed clozapine at discharge, and the authors note that even this likely flatters routine care, since hospitals that actively screen also prescribe more. The 28.6% is not a population prevalence, and the paper is explicit about why. Only 52.2% of patients were assessed at all, and those who were came disproportionately from university and private hospitals rather than public ones, so the figure describes the screened subgroup rather than everyone with schizophrenia. Every institution was also authorised to prescribe clozapine, which excludes the hospitals least equipped to recognise resistance, and all were inpatients, so nothing here speaks to outpatient care.

title: Germany prescribes mental-health apps. The evidence behind them is rated "very low."
blurb: A meta-analysis of the eight prescription-eligible depression and anxiety apps in Germany found a moderate benefit for depression (SMD = -0.49) but graded that evidence "very low" quality, and for generalized anxiety the pooled result came from just two trials and was not statistically significant.
summary: Since 2020, German doctors have been able to prescribe digital health applications, known as DiGAs, the way they prescribe drugs, with statutory insurance covering the cost. Researchers led by A. Schmitz asked what the evidence actually shows. They searched the official DiGA directory, found eight permanently listed apps targeting depression or generalized anxiety disorder, and pooled the 19 randomised trials behind them. For depression, apps beat control conditions by a standardised mean difference of -0.49 (95% CI -0.65 to -0.32) across 3,869 participants, a moderate effect that held up at follow-up (-0.35) and is comparable in size to what face-to-face therapy trials report. The authors are careful to say that comparability is not equivalence, because no trial has ever directly compared the two. For generalized anxiety the pooled estimate was -2.31, but its confidence interval ran from -5.32 to 0.70, meaning the data cannot rule out harm, and it rests on two trials and 295 people. The team graded their own evidence using GRADE, a standard system for rating confidence in a result, and the verdict is the story: "very low" for depression at the end of treatment and "very low" for anxiety, downgraded for missing blinding, high dropout and inconsistency between studies. Three further details deserve weight. Twelve of the nineteen trials evaluated a single app, Deprexis, so the pooled figure is not evenly representative of the eight. About 20% of participants were also in psychotherapy and about 30% were taking psychiatric medication, so these are not effects of an app alone. And the average participant was 38.7 years old with no data at all on people over 70, while non-German speakers and those with less education were underrepresented -- the groups for whom a prescription app is often argued to matter most.

title: Borderline personality disorder and the body: what 4 weeks of DBT changed
blurb: Patients with BPD paid markedly less attention to internal body signals than controls (MAIA-2 2.10 vs 2.87), and that gap tracked their interpersonal problems. After four weeks of residential DBT, only their self-reported attention improved -- the brain and heartbeat measures did not budge.
summary: Interoception is the sense of your own body from the inside: a racing heart, a tight chest, the physical signature of an emotion. Because borderline personality disorder involves intense emotional swings and a disturbed sense of self, researchers have long suspected interoception is part of the picture, but "interoception" is really several different abilities. Researchers led by Jella Voelter separated two of them in BPD patients and healthy controls: accuracy, tested with a heartbeat discrimination task, and attention, measured by questionnaire and by fMRI while participants focused on their heartbeat. The two came apart cleanly. Accuracy was no different between groups overall, though it fell as BPD symptom severity rose. Attention was clearly reduced: BPD patients scored 2.10 on the MAIA-2 attention measure against 2.87 for controls, and the lower their score, the more interpersonal problems they reported. The brain data matched: in the insula and dorsal anterior cingulate, regions that integrate body signals, BPD patients showed less separation between attending inward to the heartbeat and attending outward, as though the switch between the two were blunted. Then 37 patients completed a four-week residential DBT programme and were retested. Self-reported interoceptive attention improved. Nothing else did -- not the brain response, not the heartbeat task. The authors read this as evidence that interoceptive disturbance in BPD is specific to attention, and that self-report and physiology respond to treatment on different timelines, noting that mindfulness effects on interoception usually take about eight weeks to appear while this programme ran four. The design limits what follows from it: there was no waiting-list patient group, so improvement over four weeks cannot be separated from time and residential care generally. The patients were a naturalistic sample with comorbidities and psychiatric medication, included as a statistical control rather than excluded, and the heartbeat task was difficult even for controls, which may hide real differences rather than show their absence.

title: Finland put 7-session internet CBT for social anxiety into routine care. Did it work?
blurb: Across 1,654 physician-referred patients nationwide, a free 7-session therapist-guided internet CBT programme produced a large improvement in social anxiety (d = 1.09), with 41.1% improving reliably and 1.7% getting reliably worse -- but there was no control group.
summary: Internet-delivered CBT for social anxiety works in trials. Whether it works in an ordinary health service, where nobody is screened into a study and people drop out for their own reasons, is a different question. Helsinki University Hospital runs a nationwide programme, and researchers led by Anna Paula Laizane examined its register from 2019 to 2022: 1,654 adults across Finland, all referred by a physician rather than self-referred, all scoring at least 21 on the Social Phobia Inventory, treated free of charge in seven therapist-supported sessions on a flexible schedule. On the primary social anxiety measure the improvement was large, d = 1.09 overall and d = 1.15 among those who finished, with smaller gains for people who left late (d = 0.72) or early (d = 0.41). Patients improved by about 2.2 points every other session. Using a threshold of a 10-point change as reliable, 41.1% improved reliably and 1.7% got reliably worse; 19.9% ended in the subclinical range, rising to 30.2% among completers. Adherence was good for a digital programme: an average of 5.74 of 7 sessions, and 54% finished. The authors argue the short course is part of why. The honest limit is stated in the paper: there is no control group, so the specific effect of the therapy cannot be separated from the natural course of the condition or from simply being in care. Two design choices cut both ways. No diagnostic interview was done at screening, which made the programme cheaper to scale but means the diagnosis rests on the referring physician plus a questionnaire cutoff. And restricting entry to more severe cases, along with the fact that people who completed treatment started out slightly older with less depression, means the completer figures describe a self-selected group rather than everyone referred.

title: In addiction treatment, shame predicted suicidal thinking. Depression was the link.
blurb: Among 265 people in treatment for substance use disorder in Turkiye, self-stigma predicted suicide-related thinking, and of depression, anxiety and stress, only depression carried the effect. Perceived social support weakened the link at every level tested.
summary: Self-stigma is what happens when a person absorbs society's judgement about their condition and turns it inward, and in addiction it is unusually potent because the public narrative treats the condition as a moral failing. Researchers led by Zehra Ucar Hasanli asked whether that internalised shame connects to suicidal thinking, and if so, through what. They recruited 270 consecutive patients in treatment at an addiction centre affiliated with Ankara Training and Research Hospital, analysing 265, and had them complete measures of substance-use self-stigma, depression, anxiety and stress, perceived social support, and suicide-related cognitions. Self-stigma predicted all three forms of distress. But when depression, anxiety and stress were tested together as competing explanations, only depression predicted suicide cognitions (b = 0.78, p = .012); anxiety and stress both fell away entirely. The indirect path from self-stigma through depression was statistically significant, and the direct path survived too, meaning depression carries part of the effect but not all of it. Social support mattered at every level tested: for people reporting strong support from a partner or significant other, the slope linking self-stigma to suicide cognitions was roughly a third of what it was for those reporting weak support. The design caps what can be claimed. This is a single snapshot in time, so calling depression a "mediator" describes a statistical pattern, not a demonstrated sequence -- shame could follow low mood as easily as cause it. Every measure was self-report, raising the risk that one person's response style colours all of their answers. Depression, anxiety and stress were highly intercorrelated, which the authors flag as a reason the anxiety and stress paths may have been washed out rather than genuinely absent. And the sample was 92% men, drawn from one clinic and excluding alcohol use disorder deliberately, so it describes men in treatment for illicit substance use in one Turkish city.

title: ICU diaries are meant to prevent PTSD. Correcting for publication bias, they didn't.
blurb: A meta-analysis of 21 studies and 2,180 ICU survivors found that once results were adjusted for publication bias, ICU diaries had no statistically significant effect on PTSD incidence (RR 0.73, CI 0.47-1.12) or severity. Modest benefits for anxiety and depression survived.
summary: Many intensive care patients come away with fragmented, sometimes delusional memories of their stay, and a widespread nursing intervention tries to help: staff and families keep a diary during the admission that the patient can later read to rebuild a coherent account. It is cheap, humane, and widely believed to reduce post-ICU PTSD. Researchers led by Wenyu Zhang tested that belief across seven databases, pooling 21 controlled studies (17 randomised, 4 not) covering 2,180 survivors, and did something most earlier reviews skipped: they formally corrected for publication bias, the tendency for studies finding nothing to go unpublished. Before adjustment, the picture looked favourable, and a trial sequential analysis crossed the boundary for benefit. After trim-and-fill correction, it did not hold. PTSD incidence gave a risk ratio of 0.73 with a confidence interval from 0.47 to 1.12, which includes no effect at all, and PTSD severity gave a standardised mean difference of -0.23 with an interval from -1.20 to 0.75, consistent with meaningful harm or meaningful benefit. Modest benefits for anxiety and depression symptoms did survive the correction, and a subgroup analysis suggested diaries written by healthcare professionals without family involvement worked better for PTSD severity than family-written ones. The authors' own conclusion is appropriately narrow: diaries belong in a broader post-ICU support package, not as a standalone treatment for any one outcome. Several caveats limit how far even the null result travels. Heterogeneity ranged from 0% to 95%, so the studies frequently disagreed. Nobody can be blinded to whether they received a diary, which builds in performance bias. The subgroup comparisons used unadjusted data, so they inherit the same publication bias found in the main result. And a substantial share of the studies came from Chinese databases, where ICU visiting policies and family involvement differ from Western practice.

title: Does semaglutide protect thinking in psychiatric patients? 13,007 records say maybe
blurb: In a retrospective study of 13,007 US patients with psychiatric diagnoses, those starting semaglutide had fewer recorded cognitive problems at 12 months than those on no diabetes drug (mean score 11.1 vs 14.9). But semaglutide was no better than sitagliptin, which undercuts the drug-specific explanation.
summary: Cognitive problems -- fogginess, poor memory, trouble concentrating -- run through most psychiatric conditions and respond poorly to existing treatment. Semaglutide, the GLP-1 drug sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, has hinted at cognitive benefits in diabetes and obesity, so researchers led by Riccardo De Giorgi asked whether the same shows up in psychiatric populations. Using NeuroBlu, a database of de-identified US electronic health records, they identified 13,007 adults with a psychiatric diagnosis who had a routine clinician-rated cognitive assessment both before and after starting a diabetes drug, then compared semaglutide against sitagliptin, empagliflozin, glipizide and no treatment. At 12 months, people on semaglutide had a mean cognitive-problem score of 11.1 against 14.9 for those on no diabetes drug, a difference that held against glipizide and empagliflozin too, and was clearest in memory. The catch is in the fourth comparison: semaglutide was statistically indistinguishable from sitagliptin. The authors take that seriously, suggesting both drugs may help by improving blood-sugar control rather than through anything specific to semaglutide -- and noting this contradicts findings in the general diabetes population, where semaglutide did beat sitagliptin. Attention and orientation showed no difference at all. Three limits matter most. This is observational, so people prescribed semaglutide differ from those who were not in ways the records do not capture -- NeuroBlu holds no socioeconomic status, insurance status or lifestyle data. "Cognition" here means descriptions a clinician typed during a routine appointment, not a cognitive test, which is far coarser than it sounds. And requiring an assessment both before and after treatment selected for patients with more clinical contact and more cognitive concern, while cognitive assessments were actually less frequent during semaglutide exposure, forcing the analysis to lean more heavily on imputed values.

title: ICD-11 makes clinicians rate personality traits as present or absent. Can they?
blurb: 133 Danish clinicians rated 238 patients' ICD-11 personality trait domains both as present/absent and on a 0-4 scale. The yes/no ratings tracked a validated measure moderately well (r = .51 to .57) -- except for Negative Affectivity, where the correlation fell to .27.
summary: ICD-11 rebuilt personality disorder diagnosis around severity plus up to five trait domains: negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition and anankastia. The domains are conceived as dimensions -- traits people have more or less of -- but the coding system only lets a clinician mark each one present or absent. Researchers led by Gunnar Valdemar Grunert asked what is lost in that compression. They invited around 2,500 clinicians in Danish Mental Health Services; 133 provided complete data, each rating a patient (238 in total, 73% women, average age 33) three ways: a present/absent judgement, a 0-to-4 judgement, and the Informant Personality Inventory for ICD-11, a validated questionnaire serving as the yardstick. The yes/no ratings held up better than one might fear, correlating .51 to .57 with the validated measure across four domains -- moderate, and statistically robust after correction for multiple testing. Negative affectivity was the exception, managing only .27, which the authors flag as the domain where a binary judgement loses most. The 0-to-4 ratings did better overall (.40 to .75), but once corrected for multiple comparisons, only disinhibition and dissociality were significantly better captured dimensionally. Neither years of experience nor professional background predicted who rated more accurately. One feature of the design should temper all of this, and the authors name it: the same clinician produced both the single-item ratings and the criterion questionnaire, so shared method variance -- one person's impression of a patient colouring every measure they complete -- likely inflates the agreement. Recruitment was voluntary and open-ended, which the authors think probably attracted clinicians already interested in personality pathology, inflating estimates further. And the patients were a broad mental-health sample rather than a personality disorder sample, so it remains untested whether severity makes a binary call easier or harder.

title: States spend more on suicide prevention than they used to. Not where the deaths are.
blurb: Across 306 enacted state budgets for 2021-2026, states explicitly allocated $7.2 billion to suicide prevention and crisis services, rising from $1.05 to $6.55 per person. But 21.6% of state-years allocated nothing, and a state's suicide rate bore no relationship to what it budgeted.
summary: The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline launched nationally in 2022, but the infrastructure behind it -- call centres, mobile crisis teams, stabilisation units -- is largely built and paid for by individual states. Researchers led by Jonathan Purtle read every enacted state budget for fiscal years 2021 through 2026, 306 in all, and counted the dollars explicitly labelled for suicide prevention and crisis services. The total was $7.2 billion, and the trend was up: mean per capita funding climbed from $1.05 in 2021 to $6.55 in 2025, with the share of total state budgets rising alongside it. Two findings complicate the good news. First, the spending is wildly uneven and often absent -- the median state-year allocated $0.87 per person, a fraction of the $3.63 mean, and in 66 of the 306 state-years, 21.6% of them, the figure was exactly zero. Second, and most striking, there was no significant association between a state's suicide death rate and how much it budgeted. Need, measured the most direct way available, did not predict funding. What did predict it was legislation: states that had enacted a 988 telecom fee, a small surcharge on phone bills, budgeted more than twice as much per person as states that had not ($7.73 versus $3.13), which the authors offer as a practical financing route. The study counts only money a budget explicitly labels for this purpose, so it undercounts the real total -- city and county funding, general mental health spending and Medicaid crisis services all sit outside it, and by amounts that likely differ state to state. It also counts dollars budgeted rather than dollars spent, and actual expenditure is usually lower. Because suicide rates were measured before each fiscal year, nothing here can say whether the additional money changed outcomes.

title: CBT cut OCD symptoms sharply -- and changed a brain signal for holding back
blurb: In a randomized trial of 60 adults with OCD, 77.8% of those receiving 12 CBT sessions met response criteria versus 7.7% on the waitlist, and 37% reached remission. The brain's No-Go P3 signal, an electrical marker of inhibition, increased alongside.
summary: Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is the established psychological treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder, but what it changes in the brain is unsettled. One candidate is response inhibition, the ability to stop an action before you take it, which is measurably weaker in OCD and maps neatly onto the experience of not being able to resist a compulsion. Researchers led by Metin Cinaroglu randomised 60 adults meeting DSM-5 criteria for OCD to 12 individual CBT sessions or a waitlist, and measured both symptoms and EEG during a Go/No-Go task, in which participants press a button for one cue and must withhold it for another. Fifty-three completed both assessments. The clinical results were decisive: 21 of 27 in the CBT group (77.8%) met the standard response threshold of a 35% Y-BOCS reduction, against 2 of 26 on the waitlist (7.7%), and 10 (37%) reached remission, the group moving from the moderate-to-severe range into the mild range. Obsessive beliefs and intolerance of uncertainty dropped in parallel. The electrophysiology moved as predicted too, with the No-Go P3 -- a brain response around 300 to 600 milliseconds after a stop cue, read as the signature of active inhibition -- increasing in amplitude after treatment. That the symptoms improved is not in doubt; the brain interpretation needs more care. The control was a waitlist, not an active therapy, so expectancy, therapist attention and simple engagement are not controlled for, and repeating the same Go/No-Go task invites practice effects that could produce part of the change. The clinician scoring symptom severity knew who had been treated. The EEG used a 14-channel portable headset, which the authors are careful to say supports scalp-level claims only, not statements about specific brain regions. And with 53 completers from a single cultural setting, no follow-up beyond the end of treatment, and no healthy comparison group, it is unknown whether the signal normalised or merely shifted.

title: A workplace stress app cut distress scores in half. The control group got worse.
blurb: In a 4-week randomized trial of 201 working adults, distress scores fell from 29.1 to 14.6 in the app group -- but rose from 20.3 to 23.6 in the control group, and 21 people quit the app arm against 2 in the control arm.
summary: Work stress is one of the most common routes into anxiety and depression, and one of the least well served, particularly where therapy is expensive or stigmatised. Researchers led by Sisi Li tested Neurum, a smartphone tool built on ecological momentary intervention -- the idea of delivering a short CBT, mindfulness or self-regulation exercise in the moment, in the middle of an ordinary working day, rather than in a weekly appointment. They randomised 201 working adults to four weeks of the app or to a control condition, measuring distress with the DASS-21. The headline result is genuinely large: intervention-group scores fell from 29.1 to 14.6, roughly halving, with a large statistical interaction between group and time. Two features of how that number was produced deserve equal billing. First, the control group did not merely fail to improve -- it deteriorated, from 20.3 to 23.6. Part of the gap between groups therefore comes from the comparison condition getting worse, not from the app making people better, and the trial ran during a period of local social unrest and the COVID-19 pandemic, which plausibly explains a drifting control group. Second, attrition was strikingly one-sided: 21 people left the app group against 2 from the control group, a difference the authors attribute to how demanding repeated in-the-moment logging is. The people most likely to find the app burdensome are exactly the ones removed from its results. Actual use was modest -- an average of 9.74 mood journals, 6.27 exercises and about five minutes a day -- and the authors report no dose-response relationship, meaning people who used the app more did not improve more, which is hard to square with the app being the active ingredient. There was no active control, ethnicity was not recorded, and follow-up ended with the intervention, so nothing here speaks to whether the gains lasted.

title: Poverty predicted teen depression. Brain scans didn't -- and that's the finding.
blurb: Following 206 Mexican-origin youth from age 10 to 18, lower family income predicted larger amygdala and hippocampal volumes, and teens' own sense of hardship predicted depression. But brain volume predicted no depression at all, and the mediation model fit worse than one without it.
summary: A widely held account of how poverty damages mental health runs through the brain: chronic financial stress alters the development of emotion-regulating regions, and those altered regions produce depression. Researchers led by Brandon K. Hayes tested that chain end to end in the California Families Project, following 206 Mexican-origin adolescents with annual measures of family income and economic hardship from age 10 to 16, an MRI scan at 17, and a depression assessment at 18. Each link was examined separately, and the results split apart. Poverty did relate to brain structure: lower average income relative to family need predicted larger amygdala and hippocampal volumes, while teenagers' own reports of hardship predicted a smaller anterior cingulate cortex. Hardship did relate to depression -- but only when the teenagers reported it themselves. And the middle link failed entirely: none of the four brain regions predicted depressive symptoms, the indirect effects through them were not significant, and when the researchers tested a stripped-down model with the mediation removed, that simpler model fit the data better. Parent-reported hardship, the measure the primary analyses were built on, was unrelated to both brain volume and depression. The teenagers' own perception of their family's finances was the only thing that predicted how depressed they were at 18. Several limits are worth naming. The sample was recruited into the neuroimaging sub-study on the basis of depression risk, so it is not a general population. The brain was measured once, at 17, which makes it a snapshot standing in for a developmental process. The depression measure was switched from the preregistered one because attrition had left too little data, a deviation the authors document. And the youth-reported hardship analysis was added after the fact, once the planned model had come up empty -- which is the honest way to report it, but makes it a hypothesis for the next study rather than a result to bank.

title: Tai chi "ranked best" for depression in older adults. It didn't beat anything.
blurb: A network meta-analysis of 23 trials and 1,485 older adults ranked Tai Chi first for depressive symptoms (SUCRA 83.3%). But every head-to-head comparison between exercise types was statistically non-significant, with intervals as wide as -7.02 to 6.00.
summary: Mind-body exercise is an appealing option for depression in later life: low intensity, little equipment, no drug interactions. The open question is whether the particular practice matters, so researchers led by Zaiwen Wang ran a network meta-analysis -- a method that can compare treatments never tested against each other by linking them through shared comparisons -- across 23 randomised trials covering 728 older adults in intervention groups and 757 in control groups, all averaging over 63 years old. The rankings that came out are the part likely to be quoted: Tai Chi first with a SUCRA of 83.3%, then Pilates, Yoga, Qigong and Square Dancing. Read the comparisons underneath and the ranking dissolves. Tai Chi versus Pilates gave a standardised mean difference of -0.51 with a confidence interval from -7.02 to 6.00. Against Yoga, -1.22 (-5.87 to 3.42). Against Qigong, -1.81 (-5.84 to 2.22). Every interval crosses zero, several by an enormous margin, meaning the data cannot distinguish these practices from one another at all. The only statistically significant finding in the network was Qigong against no intervention (-4.00, -7.32 to -0.68). A SUCRA value is a probability of ranking highly, not a measure of how much better something is, and the authors say so directly, warning that their network was unbalanced and sparse and that the results show "estimated trends and uncertainty rather than definitive superiority." One further limitation is unusually consequential here and the authors flag it themselves: the review searched only English-language databases, excluding Chinese ones, while three of the five interventions compared -- Tai Chi, Qigong and Square Dancing -- are practices whose trials are disproportionately published in Chinese. The defensible takeaway is that gentle group exercise beats doing nothing, and that picking between the types is not yet supported by evidence.

title: Being treated badly predicted rising drinking -- unless self-control was quick
blurb: Following 133 college students for three years, those reporting more social mistreatment showed steeper increases in alcohol problems. Faster response inhibition on a lab task blunted that link -- but the crucial three-way test was not significant (p = 0.10).
summary: Being belittled, excluded or treated unfairly is a reliable predictor of heavy drinking, but not everyone responds that way, and researchers led by Chia-Chuan Yu asked whether the difference lies in self-regulation. They followed 133 college students for three years, measuring alcohol problems annually with the AUDIT and social mistreatment alongside it, and at baseline put everyone through a Stop-Signal Task in an MRI scanner. That task yields two measures: stop-signal reaction time, essentially how fast someone can cancel an action already underway, and post-error slowing, how much they pause after getting one wrong. Drinking problems rose across the three years, and the rise was steeper for students reporting more mistreatment, a significant interaction adding about 2.67% of explained variance. Inhibition mattered too: students with faster stop-signal times showed flatter drinking trajectories, and there was a significant interaction between inhibition and mistreatment, suggesting quicker self-control blunted the effect of being treated badly. The interpretation needs restraint on exactly the point that makes the finding interesting. The three-way test -- whether inhibition changes how mistreatment shapes drinking over time -- came out non-significant at p = 0.10. So the moderation is visible in the cross-section but not confirmed in the trajectory, and the authors describe the brain-behaviour analyses as exploratory throughout. They also note their p-threshold was an uncorrected 0.05 across a set of candidate moderators, which inflates the chance of a false positive. Other limits are worth carrying into any reading of it: these were relatively healthy college students, not people with diagnosed alcohol use disorder; the sample was 64.7% female and the imbalance widened at follow-up; and the mistreatment measure does not distinguish its source, so sexism, racism and ordinary interpersonal unpleasantness are pooled into one score despite plausibly acting differently.

title: The invisible work of running a household: who carries it, and what it costs
blurb: Across two German surveys of 368 women and 1,871 mothers, women reported doing 84.2% of the invisible household work -- planning, organising, remembering -- against 69.4% of the visible tasks. Mental load correlated with negative affect (r = .36), anxiety (.33) and depression (.26).
summary: "Mental load" names the part of running a household that leaves no trace: remembering the dentist appointment, noticing the shoes have got too small, holding the whole schedule in your head. Researchers led by Stefanie M. Jungmann ran two German online surveys -- 368 women, then 1,871 mothers -- to separate that invisible work from the visible kind and ask what it costs. The split was stark: women reported handling 84.2% of invisible tasks against 69.4% of visible ones, so the inequality is not in the cooking and cleaning but in the thinking behind them. They were also significantly more dissatisfied with how invisible work was divided, and that dissatisfaction belonged almost entirely to mothers: women without children reported essentially no difference between the two kinds of task. The reasons people gave were consistent, and revealing -- the most common were that the work is never finished and simply repeats, that there is too much of it, and that it leaves no break or time for oneself. Mental load tracked with worse mental health: positive affect fell slightly, while negative affect correlated at r = .36, generalised anxiety at .33 and depressive symptoms at .26, all modest-to-moderate associations. Two limits shape what this can support. Both studies are single snapshots, so nothing establishes direction -- carrying more invisible work might raise anxiety, or being anxious might make the same workload feel heavier, and the data cannot separate those. And recruitment ran through university mailing lists, Instagram, X and parent forums with no incentive, which selects for women who already recognise "mental load" as describing their life. The percentages should therefore be read as describing this self-selected group, not as a population estimate of how German households divide labour. Notably, some participants reported no burden at all.

title: Only 19.3% of Dutch forensic outpatients had a personality disorder diagnosis
blurb: Across 15 institutions and 10,560 people in Dutch outpatient forensic mental health, 19.3% carried a personality disorder diagnosis -- below rates in general psychiatric outpatient and detention settings. Of specific diagnoses, 71.2% were "other specified" or unspecified.
summary: In forensic mental health, a personality disorder diagnosis is not a label for its own sake: it shapes risk assessment, what treatment is offered, and how recidivism is managed. Researchers led by Barbera E. Van Reijswoud collected, from fifteen Dutch outpatient forensic institutions, diagnoses for everyone treated in 2023, a total of 10,560 people, to establish how often personality pathology is actually recorded. It was recorded for 19.3%, or 2,033 individuals: 12% with a personality disorder as their primary diagnosis and 7.3% carrying one only as an additional diagnosis. The authors read that as too low rather than reassuring, since systematic reviews put rates in general psychiatric outpatient and detention populations considerably higher, and they conclude personality pathology is under-recognised in this setting. A second pattern supports the interpretation. Among those given a specific diagnosis, 71.2% were coded as "other specified" or unspecified personality disorder -- a placeholder rather than a description -- with borderline (12.4%) and antisocial (11.5%) the only named categories above 2%. Over half of the people whose primary diagnosis was a personality disorder were coded with nothing more precise than the general category. Diagnoses were more common among women, middle-aged patients, those in voluntary rather than mandated treatment, and those involved in more serious violent offences. The measurement caveat is large and the authors state it. The fifteen institutions supplied data of differing completeness: six provided only primary diagnoses, and four -- accounting for 61% of all individuals -- reported only broad DSM categories rather than specific ones. Nothing was recorded about how any diagnosis was reached, so structured assessment cannot be distinguished from clinical impression. This is a study of what gets written down, which is precisely the point, but it means the 19.3% is a floor on prevalence, not a measurement of it.
authors: Barbera E. Van Reijswoud, et al.

title: A digital CBT programme cut nurse burnout. The suicide finding was weaker than billed.
blurb: In a randomized trial of 501 at-risk US nurses, adding a video-based CBT skills programme to mental-health screening significantly reduced burnout at 6 months (RRR 0.698). The reduction in suicidal ideation did not reach statistical significance, though the paper's conclusion highlights it.
summary: Burnout and distress among nurses are severe enough to be described as occupational epidemics, and screening programmes are the common response -- but screening only identifies people, it does not treat them. Researchers led by Bernadette Mazurek Melnyk tested whether adding something to the screening helps. They randomised 501 at-risk nurses recruited across US professional organisations and health systems to psychologically safe mental-health screening and referral alone, or the same plus MINDBODYSTRONG, a seven-session video-based cognitive-behavioural skills programme, then followed them for six months. On anxiety, stress and healthy-lifestyle measures the added programme did better, though the effects were small by conventional standards (absolute d of 0.06 to 0.35). The clearest result was burnout: at six months, nurses in the programme had a significantly lower risk than those who got screening alone (relative risk ratio 0.698, 95% CI 0.528 to 0.929). Engagement with the video sessions was high, with 71% completing all seven, though only 37.4% finished the skills-building activities that follow each one. On suicidal ideation the honest reading differs from the paper's own framing. Risk fell in the programme group and the six-month estimate looks substantial (RRR 0.329), but its confidence interval runs from 0.101 to 1.072 and therefore includes no effect at all. The authors state in their results that the suicidality effects did not reach statistical significance, yet their conclusion describes reduced suicidal ideation and its potential life-saving impact. The burnout finding stands; the suicide claim does not yet. Three further limits: all outcomes were self-reported, suicidal ideation was measured with a single PHQ-9 item rather than a dedicated instrument, and the sample was over 80% non-Hispanic white and over 80% degree-educated, recruited by combining random and convenience sampling. No dose-response relationship appeared for the continuous outcomes.

title: An AI therapist in VR matched ordinary CBT -- with 20 students per group
blurb: In a 3-arm trial of 60 Chinese university students, both a large-language-model VR CBT system and face-to-face CBT beat minimal support for academic anxiety. Traditional CBT's advantage was numerically larger, but the difference between them was not significant (p = 0.103).
summary: If a language model can deliver cognitive behavioural therapy, the bottleneck of therapist availability in university counselling services starts to look solvable. Researchers led by Hao Fang built a system combining virtual reality, a large language model and retrieval-augmented generation -- a method that grounds the model's replies in a specific set of documents, here CBT material, rather than letting it improvise -- and tested it against the real thing. Sixty students at a university in Wuhan with mild or moderate academic anxiety were randomly assigned, twenty per arm, to the system, to face-to-face CBT, or to minimal support, for four weekly 50-minute sessions. Both active treatments beat minimal support on academic anxiety and on heart rate, with large group-by-time interactions. Skin temperature, also measured, showed nothing. The comparison everyone will care about is the one between the two therapies, and it needs stating precisely. The difference in change scores was 2.05 points favouring traditional CBT, and it was not statistically significant (p = 0.103). That is not evidence the two are equivalent: with twenty students per arm this trial had no realistic power to detect a difference of that size, so reading the result as parity conflates no difference found with no difference exists. The point estimate, if anything, favours the human. The authors are unusually candid about the study's standing, calling it a preliminary exploratory single-centre trial and stating that it was not prospectively registered on any public trial registry. Participants could not be blinded, given the obvious difference between wearing a VR headset and sitting with a therapist, though assessors and statisticians were. Follow-up ended with the intervention, so nothing is known beyond six weeks. And safety events and system malfunctions were not tracked as prespecified endpoints, which the authors list as a limitation of their own design.

title: ADHD medication varies sixfold across Danish towns. Nobody can explain why.
blurb: Across Danish municipalities in 2024, ADHD medication among 4-17 year-olds ranged from 9.6 to 58 per 1,000 children, with diagnoses varying in parallel. Municipal wealth, hospital waiting times and private specialist supply all failed to account for it.
summary: Whether a child is diagnosed with ADHD and prescribed medication ought to depend on the child. Researchers led by Heidi Sonne used Denmark's national registers -- which cover every resident, with pharmacy records capturing every dispensed prescription regardless of who wrote it -- to see whether it also depends on where they live. Across the country's municipalities in 2024, medication prevalence among 4-to-17-year-olds ranged from 9.6 per 1,000 children in parts of Funen to 58 per 1,000 in parts of North and Central Denmark, roughly a sixfold spread, and diagnoses followed the same geography (15 to 74 per 1,000). The gap widened with age: among 13-to-17-year-olds, medication ranged from 12 to 94 per 1,000 and diagnoses from 22 to 113 per 1,000, meaning that in some municipalities more than one adolescent in ten carried a diagnosis while in others it was closer to one in forty-five. The interesting part is what failed to explain it. The team tested three plausible accounts. Municipal socioeconomic need showed only a borderline inverse association with medication (rho = -0.20, p = 0.049) and none at all with diagnoses. Regional hospital waiting times showed nothing. Private child-psychiatrist capacity showed nothing. The authors are careful about the one association they did find, noting that they ran many correlations without correcting for multiple comparisons, so a p-value of 0.049 should not be leaned on. Two measurement issues shape the nulls. Diagnoses made by private practising child psychiatrists do not enter the national patient registry, though the authors cite evidence that 91% of capturable diagnoses were recorded in the hospital sector. More importantly, the outcomes were measured across 98 municipalities while waiting times and specialist capacity were available only for 5 regions -- a mismatch in resolution that the authors say may itself explain why those factors came out null. The variation is real and well measured; its cause remains open.

title: How many people fear dementia? After 56 studies, the answer is that we can't tell.
blurb: A systematic review of 56 studies across four continents found reported rates of dementia fear ranging from 12.7% to 68.0% -- figures the authors say should not be treated as directly comparable, because almost every study used a different instrument and threshold.
summary: Fear of developing dementia shapes real behaviour: whether someone mentions memory lapses to a doctor, agrees to cognitive screening, or avoids the subject entirely. Researchers led by Feng Chen set out to establish how common that fear is among adults who do not have a dementia diagnosis, searching eight databases including four Chinese-language ones, and including 56 studies from mainland China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, the US, the UK, Germany and Israel. The reported figures ranged from 12.7% to 68.0%. That spread is the finding rather than a nuisance around it. The 12.7% came from a single-item question about severe fear put to German adults aged 40 to 70; the 68.0% came from moderate-to-high scores on the Fear of Dementia Scale among older adults in Chinese long-term care institutions. Different constructs, different instruments, different cut-offs, different populations -- and the authors say plainly that these should not be interpreted as directly comparable prevalence estimates, concluding that the evidence does not permit a reliable estimate at all. Their assessment of the measures themselves explains why. Judged against COSMIN, the standard framework for rating health measurement instruments, most scales reported internal consistency and factor structure, but evidence for content validity, cross-cultural measurement invariance, measurement error and responsiveness was limited or absent. In other words, the instruments have not been shown to mean the same thing in different languages and cultures, which is exactly what a cross-country prevalence comparison assumes. What did hold up more consistently, supported mainly by studies the reviewers rated high quality, is that anxiety and depression accompany greater fear of dementia, while social support and good family functioning accompany less -- though the latter rests on only two studies. Fear was higher among people in long-term care, hospitalised older patients, rural older adults, and anyone with memory complaints or a family history of dementia. Most of the 56 studies were cross-sectional, so none of this establishes which way the arrow points.
